title: “LOVE IS PATIENT, LOVE IS KIND” WASN’T WRITTEN JUST FOR WEDDINGS
paragraphs: “LOVE IS PATIENT, LOVE IS KIND” WASN’T WRITTEN JUST FOR WEDDINGS

We put these words on wedding programs, wooden signs, and anniversary cards. Paul wrote them to confront Christians—and if you read what comes next slowly enough, you may discover that the person God wants to change is not the person who hurt you.
You have probably heard the words while two people stood at an altar.
Flowers everywhere.
Family smiling.
A bride holding back tears.
A groom trying to breathe normally.
Then someone opens a Bible and reads words almost everybody recognizes:
“Love is patient. Love is kind.”
Beautiful.
Romantic.
Perfect for a wedding.
Except there is something we have forgotten.
Paul did not originally write 1 Corinthians 13 as a wedding ceremony.
He wrote it to Christians.
Real Christians.
Gifted Christians.
Imperfect Christians.
Christians who could talk about spiritual things while still struggling to love one another.
And suddenly the chapter becomes much more uncomfortable.
Because 1 Corinthians 13 is not merely asking whether you love the person whose hand you hold at an altar.
It is asking what happens when somebody gets on your nerves.
What happens when you are overlooked.
What happens when somebody else receives the recognition you wanted.
What happens when someone disappoints you.
What happens when you have every opportunity to remind somebody of what they did to you.
What happens when you are right...
but you are not loving.
That changes the way these famous words sound.
The Greek text of 1 Corinthians 13:4 begins:
“Ἡ ἀγάπη μακροθυμεῖ, χρηστεύεται...”
Hē agapē makrothymei, chrēsteuetai...
Love is patient.
Love is kind.

The word translated “patient,” makrothymei, carries the sense of being long-suffering or persevering rather than quickly retaliating. Chrēsteuetai means to show oneself kind. Paul is describing love with verbs—with what love actually does. The Greek text then says love does not envy, boast, or become puffed up.
Read that again.
Love is not merely something you feel.
Love behaves.
And this is where the wedding verse becomes a mirror.
Because it is easy to say, “I love people.”
It is harder to ask:
Am I patient with them?
Am I kind when kindness costs me something?
What happens inside me when somebody else succeeds?
Do I secretly need recognition?
Do I keep replaying somebody's failure?
Do I punish people emotionally until I feel they have suffered enough?
Do I call bitterness “discernment”?
Do I call revenge “boundaries”?
Do I call pride “knowing my worth”?
Do I call gossip “asking for prayer”?
Do I call cruelty “telling the truth”?
That is where 1 Corinthians 13 stops decorating the wall and starts dismantling the heart.
Paul continues:
“οὐ ζηλοῖ... οὐ περπερεύεται, οὐ φυσιοῦται.”
Love does not envy.
Love does not boast.
Love is not puffed up.
And perhaps this is where someone reading this needs to stop pretending.
Because jealousy can wear church clothes.
Pride can quote Scripture.
Bitterness can sit through worship.
Resentment can raise its hands during a song.
A person can know Christian vocabulary while quietly keeping an emotional courtroom open inside the heart.
Evidence carefully stored.
Conversations remembered.
Screenshots saved.
Offenses catalogued.
Sentences rehearsed for the imaginary day when you finally get to tell them exactly what they did to you.
Then Paul goes deeper.
“οὐ ζητεῖ τὰ ἑαυτῆς... οὐ λογίζεται τὸ κακόν.”
Love does not seek its own interests.
Love does not keep an account of wrongs.
That does not mean biblical love becomes gullible.
It does not mean abuse must be tolerated.
It does not mean consequences disappear.
It does not mean reconciliation can occur without repentance, wisdom, or safety.
Forgiveness and trust are not identical.
You can forgive someone before God while recognizing that trust may need to be rebuilt through repentance, truth, and changed behavior.
And Scripture never asks us to rename evil as good.
In fact, the very next verse destroys that misunderstanding:
“οὐ χαίρει ἐπὶ τῇ ἀδικίᾳ, συγχαίρει δὲ τῇ ἀληθείᾳ.”
Love does not rejoice in unrighteousness.
Love rejoices with the truth.
Biblical love and biblical truth are not enemies.
Real love does not help somebody hide the sin destroying them.
Real love does not celebrate what God calls evil simply because confrontation feels uncomfortable.
Real love does not manipulate Scripture to keep victims silent.
Real love does not protect appearances while souls are bleeding behind closed doors.
Love rejoices in truth.
But truth without love can become a weapon in proud hands.
And love without truth can become sentimental permission for destruction.
Jesus gives us something infinitely better.
Grace and truth.
Look at Christ.
People mocked Him.
Rejected Him.
Misrepresented Him.
Spat upon Him.
Beat Him.
Stripped Him.
Nailed Him to a cross.
And the cross does not tell us that sin does not matter.
The cross tells us sin matters so much that the Son of God bore its judgment.
The cross also tells us sinners are loved so deeply that the Son of God willingly came to save His people.
That is Gospel love.
Not sentimental love.
Not Instagram-caption love.
Not wedding-decoration love.
Holy love.
Costly love.
Love with scars.
And perhaps that is why 1 Corinthians 13 can hurt so much when we stop reading it as poetry and allow it to interrogate us.
Try something uncomfortable.
Where the passage says “love,” put your own name.
“_____ is patient.”
Are you?
“_____ is kind.”
Are you?
“_____ does not envy.”
Still comfortable?
“_____ does not boast.”
“_____ is not puffed up.”
“_____ does not insist on getting his or her own way.”
“_____ does not keep a ledger of wrongs.”
At some point, most honest Christians have to stop.
Because none of us reads that mirror perfectly.
I don't.
You don't.
That realization is not meant to drive us into hopelessness.
It is meant to drive us to Jesus.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that good people finally learned how to love perfectly.
Christianity is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to the holy God through Jesus Christ.
We have failed to love.
We have been impatient.
We have spoken words we wish we could retrieve.
We have secretly enjoyed seeing someone who wounded us finally struggle.
We have envied.
Boasted.
Manipulated.
Remembered offenses selectively while forgetting how much mercy we ourselves have received.
Some of us have wanted grace for ourselves and justice for everybody else.
But then comes Jesus.
Not to congratulate our self-righteousness.
To crucify it.
Not merely to improve our manners.
To give us new life.
This is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you out of the prison of defending what is killing you.
You can finally say:
“Jesus, I was wrong.”
“I have been bitter.”
“I have been proud.”
“I have used somebody else's sin to justify my own.”
“I have demanded mercy from You while refusing mercy to others.”
“Forgive me.”
And the Gospel answers with something scandalous.
There is grace for repentant sinners.
Grace for the angry husband who finally admits his words have been cruel.
Grace for the wife whose resentment has hardened into contempt.
Grace for the parent who needs to apologize to a child.
Grace for the son who has carried hatred toward his father for years.
Grace for the daughter who learned to protect herself by never trusting anyone again.
Grace for the church member wounded by another believer.
Grace for the Christian who looks fine online and feels spiritually exhausted in private.
Grace for the person reading this thinking:
I have failed this chapter badly.
Yes.
So have the rest of us.
That is why we need Christ.
The Gospel is not “try harder until God loves you.”
The Gospel is that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
Jesus took sin seriously enough to die for it and loved sinners deeply enough to offer forgiveness through His blood.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And those who turn from sin and trust in Him are not merely given a motivational speech about becoming nicer people.
They are reconciled to God.
Forgiven.
Made new.
Then, through the Holy Spirit, Christ begins changing how redeemed people actually live.
Slowly sometimes.
Painfully sometimes.
But truly.
So maybe the question today is not:
“Who needs to love me better?”
Maybe the question that could change your life is:
“Jesus, where have I refused to love like You?”
Sit with that.
Don't rush away.
Whose name just entered your mind?
Who have you been punishing inside your imagination?
Who are you jealous of?
Who are you secretly hoping fails?
Whose apology are you demanding while refusing to acknowledge what you did?
Who needs to hear “I was wrong” from you?
Who needs your forgiveness?
Who needs a boundary established without hatred?
Who needs truth spoken without cruelty?
Who needs patience?
Who needs kindness?
And what if the Holy Spirit did not bring that person to mind so you could condemn them again...
but so Christ could deal with you?
Paul says love “πάντα στέγει, πάντα πιστεύει, πάντα ἐλπίζει, πάντα ὑπομένει”—it bears, believes, hopes, and endures.
Again, that is not permission for naïveté or abuse.
It is a portrait of persevering Christian love—a love that refuses to become evil merely because evil was done to it.
That may be one of the hardest lessons in discipleship.
What they did to you may explain your wound.
It does not have to become the author of who you become.
Jesus can rewrite what pain tried to write.
Betrayal may have written, “Never trust again.”
Jesus can write wisdom without hatred.
Abandonment may have written, “You are unwanted.”
Jesus can write, “Mine.”
Failure may have written, “Finished.”
Jesus can write, “Redeemed.”
Shame may have written, “Hide.”
Jesus can write, “Come into the light.”
Sin may have written a scandal across entire chapters of your life.
But the Gospel announces that your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Be honest.
There is no shame in admitting that discipleship is happening in unfinished people.
And if God brought a particular person to your mind while reading this, pray before you type their name anywhere. Don't publicly expose them. Let God begin with your own heart.
Not because you need another saved post.
Eventually pride will whisper again.
Eventually resentment will try to reopen an old account.
And on that day you may need to remember:
“Ἡ ἀγάπη μακροθυμεῖ, χρηστεύεται.”
Love is patient.
Love is kind.
Let the Gospel interrupt their scroll.
But hear this carefully.
Scripture does not give us permission to manipulate you that way.

Paul teaches that Christian giving is to be purposeful and willing, “not grudgingly, or of necessity,” because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7). He also speaks warmly of believers financially partnering in Gospel ministry and describes such generosity as an offering pleasing to God (Philippians 4:15–18).
Not because God needs your money.
Not because salvation can be purchased.
Not because giving earns divine favor.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The cross cannot be repaid.
But Christians can choose to financially partner with Gospel work.

And if these articles have helped you return to Scripture, confront hidden sin, seek Christ, forgive, repent, heal, pray again, or keep walking when you wanted to quit, then prayerfully consider standing with us.
Pray.
Those actions can carry truth farther than you may ever know.
Because this was never supposed to be about building an audience around us.
It is about pointing people to Him.
Jesus.
The One who loved when love cost blood.
The One who told the truth without ceasing to love.
The One who received sinners without pretending sin was harmless.
The One who carried a cross we deserved.
The One who walked out of a tomb death could not keep closed.
The One who can take proud people and teach them humility.
Bitter people and teach them forgiveness.
Wounded people and teach them how to love without surrendering truth.
Ashamed people and teach them to walk in the light.
Lost people and bring them home.
And maybe that is what you needed to hear today.
“Love is patient. Love is kind” was never meant merely to sound beautiful while two people exchange rings.
It was meant to become flesh in people who belong to Jesus.
At the kitchen table.
In the argument.
In the church conflict.
In the unanswered message.
In the family wound.
In the apology.
In the boundary.
In the forgiveness.
In the truth.
In the ordinary moments where nobody applauds you for choosing Christ over your ego.
Paul ends the chapter with faith, hope, and love remaining—and declares love the greatest.
So when the flowers are gone...
when the wedding music stops...
when feelings fluctuate...
when people disappoint you...
when your own heart disappoints you...
remember what Christian love ultimately points toward.
Not human perfection.
Christ.
The Savior whose grace meets sinners in the wreckage and refuses to leave repentant hearts where He found them.
Maybe the greatest evidence that Jesus is rewriting your story is not that nobody wounds you anymore—but that their wound no longer gets to decide who you become.
